title: Lucky John
lines: Once upon a time there was a lad, and his name was John.
This John lived with a farmer for seven whole years,
and when the seventh year was over, he said to his master:
"Master, my time is up, now I am going home to my dear mother: please pay me my wages."
"Very well, John," said the farmer,
"you have been a good lad, you served me honestly, here are your wages."
He gave him a lump of gold as big
as John's head, and even a little bigger than that.
John tied it up in a sack, put it on his shoulder and set off for home.
As he walked along, a man on horseback came toward him, and John began to sigh:
"Oh my, what a fine thing riding is!
The rider sits on his horse just like on a chair, he does not stumble on the stones,
he does not wear out his boots, and still he moves along."
The rider heard this and said to John:
"Well then, why do you go on foot?"
"Because," said John, "I have no horse.
And I must carry this gold home: I served seven years for it!
Oh, but it is heavy, my shoulder is about to break."
"Do you know what?
Let us trade," said the rider.
"I will give you the horse, and you give me the gold."
"Gladly," said John, and in that very moment he threw the sack off his shoulder.
The rider got off the horse, helped John up onto it, and even gave him good advice:
"Now, if you want to go fast, just urge it on:
gee up, gee up! and it will run like the swift wind."
Well, they wished each other God's blessing, parted, and went their two ways.
Oh, how happy John was!
Now he had a horse.
And what a horse!
He tugged at the reins and urged the horse on: gee up,
gee up! and the horse really did dash off, so fast
that John tipped now to the left, now to the right, and he tipped this way
and that, until all at once, bump! he tumbled into the ditch.
The poor fellow could hardly scramble up, his bones creaked,
every limb ached, and he was very sorry he had traded the gold for a horse.
Just as he got up, a man came along that way, driving a cow.
This man caught the horse and asked John:
"What is wrong, little brother?
The horse threw you off, did it not?"
"Oh, it did, may the wolves eat it!
Well, I will never sit on this nasty beast again.
Oh, a cow is so much better than a horse!
You can stroll quietly behind it, and it gives you milk and butter too."
"Do you know what," said the farmer, "let us trade."
"Gladly," said John.
"Better your neck gets broken than mine!"
"Do not you worry about that," said the farmer,
and with that he jumped onto the horse and galloped off like the swift wind.
John set off with the cow too, and they ambled along nice and slowly.
Oh my, how happy John was!
Now he would have no worries for the rest of his life.
If he had bread, he would have milk and butter, and cheese if he liked: what more, John?
On the way he stopped at an inn, and there he ate
what bread he had with him; he had a few pennies, so he drank some wine too,
then in a merry mood he set off again, and the two of them walked on,
they walked and walked, ambling slowly toward home.
It was getting near noon, and the heat was stifling,
and John grew so faint with thirst that his tongue hung out.
He thought to himself: here is the cow, I will milk it and my thirst will be gone.
He tied the cow to a tree, and since he had no pail with him (where would he get one?),
he took his cap, held it under the cow's udder and began to milk.
He milked and milked, but not a single drop of milk came out.
And because he wanted milk no matter what, he squeezed and tugged hard at the udder,
the cow grew tired of the joke and kicked John in the head so hard
that he fell flat on his back, lay sprawled out, and even fainted, the poor lad.
When at long last he woke up, he did not know where he was: in the sky or on the ground.
Luckily, a butcher came along that way, pushing a piglet in his wheelbarrow.
He stopped and asked John:
"What is wrong, little brother?"
John told him what had happened.
The butcher held out his flask and offered him a drink, to help him come round.
Then he looked at the cow, shook his head and said:
"You can milk this one all you like, little brother, there is not a drop of milk in her.
She is an old beast, she will never give milk again in all this world."
Oh, how sad John became!
"Well, who would have thought it," he grumbled to himself.
"What shall I do now?
Have her killed?
Who will eat the meat of this old beast?"
"Do you know what," said the butcher, "I will help you out of your trouble.
I will give you this piglet, and you give me the cow,
I will cut up her meat and somehow sell it with the rest of my meat."
"Oh, God bless you, sir!" John thanked him.
They took the piglet off the wheelbarrow,
tied a rope to its hind leg, and John set off with it.
He could hardly contain himself, he was bursting with joy to see
how lucky he was, what a good bargain he had made again!
So on they went, walking and walking.
All at once a young lad joined him, carrying a fine white goose under his arm.
They fell to talking; John told him of his great good luck,
and the lad told him he was taking the goose to a christening feast.
"Just lift it, feel how heavy it is," said the lad.
"No wonder, we fattened it for eight weeks.
Well, whoever eats this will be licking his lips afterwards, I know."
John took the goose in his hands and lifted it.
"It really is good and heavy," he said, "but my piglet is no small thing either!"
Meanwhile the lad looked around worriedly, shook his head and hummed.
Then at last he spoke up:
"Listen, my friend, you are going to get into trouble with this piglet."
"Why would I get into trouble?"
"Because I just heard in the village,
the one I came through, that someone stole a piglet from the mayor.
People are searching for it everywhere.
What if this is the stolen piglet?
I tell you truly, you will end up in prison."
Oh, how frightened John was!
He began to beg the lad to trade with him.
He would gladly give him the piglet for the goose, if only he could keep out of trouble.
The lad made him beg for a while, then, so be it, he gave John the goose,
and with the piglet he quickly turned onto a side road and swiftly vanished.
John went on his way too, turning the trade over in his mind.
"If I think it over well," he said to himself, "I made a good trade.
For one thing, this fat goose has plenty of fat; for another,
it has feathers too, we will stuff a pillow with them. Oh, how glad my mother will be!"
So John walked on and on, and when he reached the last village,
he saw an old knife grinder there, grinding busily and singing all the while:
"Round and round the wheel goes,
Money in my pocket grows.
I just grind the knives and shears,
Coins jingle in my pocket here!"
John stopped, greeted the grinder and said:
"Oh, you must have a good life, sir, to be in such a merry mood!"
"I should say so," answered the grinder.
"No man on earth has it better than a knife grinder.
He just grinds and grinds, and his pocket never empties, it is always full of money."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so.
And where did you buy that fine goose?"
"I did not buy it, I traded it for a piglet."
"For a piglet?
Is that really so?"
"It is really so."
"And where did you get the piglet?"
"I got it for a cow."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so."
"And the cow?"
"I got that for a horse."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so."
"And the horse?"
"I got that for a lump of gold as big as my head."
"Is that really so?"
"It is really so.
I could even swear to it."
"Well, listen," said the grinder, "I have seen many lucky men,
but never one like you, and I have grown old and eaten the best of my bread."
"I should say so!"
"You see, it is a pity you are not a knife grinder.
Then you would have lots of money."
"That is true," said John, "but I have no grindstone."
"Do you know what, I will give you a grindstone.
You can make a start with that.
And you give me the goose."
"Gladly, old man!" cried John with great joy.
They shook hands on it right there, and the grinder gave him a worn,
chipped grindstone, and then picked up a big stone off the ground and gave him that too:
"Here, my son, take it,
you can hammer bent nails straight with it. Use it in good health."
Well, how happy he was!
"I truly was born lucky," John said to himself as he walked along.
But all at once he grew weary, the stone grew heavier
and heavier, he was hungry and had nothing to eat;
he was thirsty and had nothing to drink. Oh dear, oh dear,
he would not have minded at all to be rid of the stones.
By blessed luck he came to a well,
there he threw down the stones and bent over the well to drink from it.
As he bent over, somehow or other, both stones went splash into the well.
"Hooray! How good!
Oh, how good!"
John jumped up with joy.
"I do not have to lug them home, oh, how good!
Well, there has never been a man in the world as lucky as I am!"
He did not stop until he got home, he ran all the way to his dear mother.
Tomorrow let John be your guest.
